paras: The masked-band attacks on Black residents of Kenton, Tennessee, were a series of raids in the autumn of 1881 in which masked men repeatedly entered the Obion County town and whipped and maltreated Black men, women and children. Residents appealed to the governor, and Governor Hawkins offered a $250 reward for the arrest and conviction of those responsible. Tennessee papers carried the raids as brief state-news items, and at least one Northern paper presented them as a remnant of the Ku Klux.

By 12 November 1881 the Milan Exchange, published at Milan in Gibson County, reported that masked men had "again" been at work in Kenton. According to the Memphis Daily Appeal, the masked men had been whipping and "otherwise maltreating colored men, women and children." The Bolivar Bulletin wrote that the town had been "frequently disturbed lately" by masked men who raided it and committed "depredations upon the colored citizens." None of the reports names a victim, gives the date of a particular raid, counts the raiders or describes injuries beyond whipping.

Kenton's residents called on the governor for help, and the governor was telegraphed about the attacks. Governor Hawkins then offered a reward of $250 for the arrest and conviction of "any of the parties concerned." No report of arrests, indictments or a trial appears in the coverage through the end of December 1881.

Only white newspapers covered the raids, each in a few lines. The Milan Exchange did not mention the victims' race, calling the raids "devilment" and advising, "Gentlemen, use your shot guns on them." The Memphis Daily Appeal placed the story among its Tennessee News items on 16 November as "some mean work," and the Bolivar Bulletin ran a similar paragraph on 24 November.

Far from Tennessee, the Daily Kennebec Journal of Augusta, Maine, printed the story in its General News column on 16 November. It introduced the item as "a fag end of ku-kluxism," the only report to tie the raids to the Ku Klux.

reader.title: Masked-band attacks on Black residents of Kenton, Tennessee
bases: A band of masked men repeatedly entered Kenton at intervals and whipped and maltreated Black men, women and children (A2, A3, A5), a recurring night-band pattern rather than a single mob action.

The Milan Exchange's local item (A1) and the Memphis Appeal and Bolivar Bulletin items (A3, A5) separately report masked men troubling Kenton and an appeal to or reward from the Governor, though A2, A3 and A5 may rest on one common report and none gives a specific incident.

accounts.gist: Masked men at Kenton were whipping and maltreating Black men, women and children, raiding the town repeatedly; the Governor offered a $250 reward.

accounts.label: Northern news brief
accounts.gist: Kenton had been visited several times by masked men who whipped and maltreated Black residents, presented as a remnant of Ku Klux activity.

framing.detail: The Milan Exchange called it 'devilment' and urged 'Gentlemen, use your shot guns on them,' without mentioning the victims' race.
The Memphis Appeal described 'some mean work' in a one-paragraph Tennessee News item; the Bolivar Bulletin spoke of 'depredations upon the colored citizens'.
The Daily Kennebec Journal in Maine framed it as 'a fag end of ku-kluxism' in a General News roundup.

record_check.dossier: 1881-11-12 (Milan Exchange); four papers, not three, reported the raids
Raids were recurring before 12 November 1881 ('again'); no specific date is given, so earlier raids may fall in October or before
Whipping and maltreatment are stated; 'depredations' is the only hint of property harm, and no property damage is described
Unnumbered Black men, women and children whipped

info: Repeated raids reported by 12 November 1881 and described as recurring ('again', 'several times', 'frequently ... lately'); no specific dates given
Unnamed Black men, women and children ('colored citizens') of Kenton
